kurz: Garum was the seasoning sauce of the Romans: fish and lots of salt, left for months until the fish's own enzymes had broken its protein down into savoury umami. This site is named after it.
bild_im_kopf: Like a house dismantled from the inside: the workers already lived there, and the salt simply locks out the looters.
was_passiert: The Romans layered small fish or fish innards with salt in vats and left them in the warmth. The large amount of salt keeps putrefying bacteria away. The digestive [[enzym|enzymes]] in the fish keep working, though, and break protein down into its building blocks ([[proteolyse|proteolysis]]). Among them is plenty of [[glutamat|glutamate]], the carrier of umami. After a few months the clear, amber liquid was skimmed off: the garum.
warum_wichtig: Garum shows that umami seasoning is no modern trick. Thai and Vietnamese fish sauce, Italian colatura di alici and Worcestershire sauce work on the same principle. Modern high-end kitchens now call any seasoning [[fermentation|fermented]] this way a garum, including ones made from meat, mushrooms or bee bread.
faustregeln: A few drops of fish sauce in tomato sauce, a braise or a dressing add depth without tasting of fish.
Fish sauce is very salty: season with it first, then add salt.
Do not ferment fish sauce yourself in the sun: without the right amount of salt and proper control, dangerous germs can grow. Use bought sauce.

stellschrauben.wirkung: The longer the enzymes work, the more protein turns into umami
Lots of salt keeps putrefaction away; too little lets it in

praxis.text: A splash of fish sauce rounds off a Bolognese, just as garum once did in Roman cooking.
Colatura di alici, made from anchovies, is the direct descendant of garum.
